It was a privilege to join thousands of shipbuilders, Navy leaders and personnel, local residents, and supporters at Bath Iron Works today for the christening of the future USS William Charette (DDG-130). This Bath-built ship is named in honor of Medal of Honor recipient Master Chief Hospital Corpsman William Charette. During the Korean War, Charette shielded a wounded Marine from an enemy grenade with his own body. Despite suffering facial wounds and shock from the blast, he improvised bandages from his clothing and continued treating wounded Marines under enemy fire. His actions were directly responsible for saving many lives. Through this ship, his courage, humility, and devotion to others will continue to inspire generations of sailors.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

The program, and others like it across our region, are supported by Congress through the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Funded separately from the summer meals program, Interfaith Human Services of Putnam provides funding so parents and guardians who accompany the participating children also receive free meals. Food Service Director Jeanette Courture is working hard to keep kids fed. This program is a real-life example of why continued federal support for meals assistance is so critical.

The contract award to Electric Boat for construction of nine Virginia submarines and five Columbia submarines is not a normal or incremental award. These are long term multi-year commitments by Congress and the Navy that will lock in work at the Groton shipyard and thousands of supply chain companies well into the late 2030s. Together, they represent the biggest shipbuilding award in modern American history.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

Fifteen years ago, on August 6, 2011, a U.S. Army CH-47D Chinook helicopter with the call sign Extortion 17 was shot down by Taliban insurgents in Afghanistan. All 38 people on board were killed, including Special Warfare Operator Senior Chief Petty Officer (SEAL) Thomas A. Ratzlaff of Green Forest and Air Force Tech. Sgt. Pararescueman John W. Brown of Siloam Springs. The downing of Extortion 17 is the largest single-incident loss of life during the War in Afghanistan. These men exemplified service and duty, sacrificing their lives in devotion to something greater than themselves—a sacrifice that speaks to their extraordinary level of character and bravery. John Brown and Thomas Ratzlaff’s legacy of courage and selfless service endures in the young men and women—many from Northwest Arkansas—who have sworn an oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic. We are forever indebted to the sacrifices made by them and the other 28 fallen American servicemembers aboard Extortion 17, and their families, and we will never forget. I enjoyed visiting Twin Knobs Dairy & Action Farms in Douglas County this week with Kaleb and Erin Rodgers to see their multi-generational operation firsthand. The Rodgers family milks 180 dairy cows while also raising beef cattle, continuing a proud farming tradition that’s been built through years of hard work and dedication. Like so many family farms across Missouri, they’re working to pass this operation on to their son, Everett, and I was excited to hear their farm is on track to earn Missouri Century Farm recognition. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, farms like Twin Knobs can count on permanent 100% immediate expensing and a permanent small business deduction, making it easier to grow, hire, and stay profitable — so operations like theirs can be passed down to Everett and the next generation. That’s the kind of certainty family farms need to keep operating for generations to come, and I’ll keep fighting for policies that provide it.

I got the chance to meet with Iron County Commissioners Josh Campbell, Jim Scaggs, and Dustin Hinkle in Ironton today to see the scale of the damage from the recent flooding. The flooding caused staggering damage across Iron County, leaving roads washed out and infrastructure damage that will cost millions of dollars to repair. County Road 65 alone took days of nonstop work just to become passable again, and that’s just one of many roads across the county still in urgent need of repair. I’m grateful for everyone who has stepped up to help Iron County rebuild, and my office will continue working to ensure this community has access to every federal resource it needs to get back on its feet.

F000466.text: I first met Doylestown’s own Allison Hamilton in Washington last October, when she joined us with The Nature Conservancy to discuss the conservation challenges facing our region. Since then, we have continued working together on several of the conservation priorities most important to our region. Chief among them is protecting the Delaware River. As Co-Chair of the Congressional Delaware River Watershed Caucus, I am leading the bipartisan effort to reauthorize and strengthen the Delaware River Basin Restoration Program—ensuring continued investments in cleaner water, restored habitats, and the local communities and economies that depend on a healthy river system. We are also working together to advance my bipartisan Safeguarding Endangered Species Act, which would overturn the Administration’s rollback of longstanding protections against habitat destruction that kills or injures threatened and endangered wildlife. The health of our environment is inseparable from the health, character, and prosperity of our communities. Allison’s local perspective, The Nature Conservancy’s expertise, and their continued partnership are indispensable to moving this work forward. Thank you to Allison and the entire TNC team for all you do for our community, our environment, and the natural resources entrusted to our care.

Join me in congratulating two outstanding young leaders from BSA Troop 71—Sam Killenbeck of Warrington and Andrew Sueta of Doylestown—on earning the rank of Eagle Scout! For his project, Sam partnered with Heritage Conservancy to design and construct four picnic tables at Lindsey Farm, including an ADA-compliant table that will help ensure visitors of all abilities can gather and enjoy this specials property. Andrew drew upon his love of American history to complete his project at the Bucks County Civil War Museum, constructing courtyard benches bookended by flower planters and creating a more welcoming setting for the outdoor presentations held there. What always stands out at a Court of Honor is that no Eagle Scout reaches this milestone alone. Speaking with Sam, Andrew, their fellow Scouts, troop leaders, friends, and families, you see the full strength of the Scouting community—young people choosing to work together and serve, and an entire village of support helping them turn that commitment into something lasting. Congratulations, Sam and Andrew—and thank you to the entire PA-1 Scouting family for continuing to lead through service!

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Richard Henry Lee was born in Virginia in 1732. At age 16, he sailed to England to continue his education. While he was studying in England, his parents died, leaving him an orphan. Returning to the colonies, Lee volunteered to raise a military company for the French and Indian War. In 1758, he was elected to the House of Burgesses. Seeking to serve his community, Lee applied to be a tax collector during the Stamp Act period. This led him to be censured and began his support for the cause for independence. While serving in the Second Continental Congress, he drafted what was known as the Lee Resolution that was used as guidance for the Declaration of Independence. He signed the Declaration in August of 1776.

2A WIN: $0 NFA tax = ZERO NFA registration! Last year, I wrote and fought for a provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill to ZERO OUT NFA taxes on suppressors and short-barreled firearms. It was my intent to also eliminate the NFA registration of these firearms, as the taxation and registration requirements are inextricably linked. M001217.text: When President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act into law on this day in 1965, he enshrined a truth that countless generations before had fought for: no American should be denied a voice in our democracy because of the color of their skin. The road to get to that moment was long and hard fought, but when that pen finally met the paper, it opened the door to a democracy closer to the promise of our founding creed: that all men are created equal. But progress is never permanent. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court weakened the very heart of this law, and state after state worked around the clock to reverse the protections that took generations to win. Let's be clear: the right to vote is not a partisan idea. It's the foundation of everything we hold near and dear to our hearts. It was won by people who believed America could be better than it was, and it falls on us to defend their legacy. We will keep that promise.

M001228.text: The State of Utah and the U.S. Forest Service are teaming up to provide $18 million to support Beaver County’s recovery.

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: Congresswoman Celeste Maloy toured the Cottonwood Fire burn scar in Beaver County today, telling KUTV's Samantha Hoffman the damage is extensive and warning that burn scar flooding remains a major concern for nearby communities. John Curtis, House Natural Resources Committee Chairman Bruce Westerman, U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz and Interior Department Senior Adviser Sam Crofts, who discussed Utah's 2026 wildfire season, forest management and efforts to reduce the risk of future catastrophic fires. 🎥 Watch @KUTV2News @samhoffmannews #Utah #BeaverCounty #CottonwoodFire #Wildfire #CelesteMaloy #JohnCurtis #FEMA #FixOurForests

Today, I was honored to welcome Speaker of the Georgia House of Representatives Jon Burns to the University of West Georgia to discuss the legacy and leadership of the late Speaker Tom Murphy. As we celebrate our country’s 250th anniversary, I am proud to honor the memory of one of the greatest Georgians to ever come from our district: the longest-serving Speaker of the Georgia House of Representatives in our state’s history, Tom Murphy. Speaker Burns and I toured Speaker Murphy’s replica office preserved in the Ingram Library, and we had an insightful discussion with Speaker Murphy’s children, former aides, and legislators who previously served in the General Assembly with him. I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act to put an end to voter disenfranchisement, but today is also a reminder that we can all do our part to lean in, participate, and protect the rights that generations of Americans fought, bled, and died for.

Chaque nouvelle attaque renforce une évidence : la Russie doit payer le prix de son agression et répondre de ses crimes. Aux côtés de l’Ukraine, nous ne céderons ni à la lassitude ni à l’intimidation. L’Union européenne et ses partenaires continueront d’accroître la pression sur la Russie, notamment par de nouvelles sanctions, tout en renforçant le soutien militaire à l’Ukraine afin qu’elle puisse se défendre et protéger sa population.

Face à la situation migratoire à Ceuta, j’ai été en contact avec le Président du gouvernement espagnol pour marquer notre solidarité et proposer toute aide nécessaire, y compris via Frontex. Je salue la coopération en cours avec le Maroc, qui a déjà permis aujourd’hui plus de 40 000 retours de Ceuta vers le Maroc. Les ministres de l’Intérieur sont en contact pour assurer un suivi étroit de la situation. Ceuta ne bénéficie pas de la libre circulation vers le reste de l’espace Schengen. J’ai toutefois demandé dès hier au Ministre de l’Intérieur de renforcer les contrôles à notre frontière avec l’Espagne si cela devait être nécessaire : 4 unités de forces mobiles, des avions et des drones sont déployés. Ces mesures viennent renforcer les dispositions que nous avons prises depuis 2020 pour mieux protéger notre frontière avec l’Espagne en étroite coordination, avec des brigades communes et une action conjointe de lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. Ces mesures viennent compléter les instruments européens adoptés pour assurer les retours et appliquer le pacte asile et migrations, avec 25% de chute des flux irréguliers vers l’Union européenne l’an dernier et une baisse poursuivie sur les routes migratoires atlantique et de Méditerranée occidentale en 2026. Solidarité et responsabilité avec nos partenaires européens pour faire appliquer nos règles de fermeté en matière de retours et de protection des frontières extérieures de l’Union. Je redis ici notre solidarité à l’Espagne, son gouvernement et son peuple.
